# Your first generated file

Twenty minutes. By the end you will have annotated a Go type,
generated code from it, broken the generated code on purpose to watch
the drift gate catch you, and deleted an output cleanly.

You need Go 1.26 and a checkout of this repository. Every command and
every output below is from a real session — if yours differs, that is
a bug worth reporting.

## 1. Build the reference binary

eidos is a framework, not a tool. What you run is a binary that
registers a set of plugins; this repository ships one that registers
twenty.

```sh
go build -o /tmp/eidos ./cmd/eidos-reference/
```

Its brand is `eidos-reference`, which is what appears in generated
headers and what names its config file. Your own tool substitutes its
own.

## 2. Get a project to generate from

Work on a copy so the repository fixture stays clean:

```sh
cp -r eidostest/testdata/demoproject /tmp/tut
cd /tmp/tut
```

Open `blog/article.go`. The interesting part is three comment lines:

```go
// +gen:repo
// +gen:builder
// +gen:register
type Article struct {
    ID    extras.UUID
    Title string
    // …
}
```

Those are **directives**. They are comments, so this package compiles
and vets normally for anyone without the tool. Each one opts `Article`
into a different generator.

## 3. Generate

```sh
/tmp/eidos run ./...
```

It prints nothing and exits `0`. Silence is success — the diagnostics
you would see are problems.

```sh
ls blog/
```

New files sit beside their sources:

```
article.go            article_builder.go    article_registry.go
article_repo.go       article_mock_test.go
comment.go            comment_builder.go
status.go             status_enum.go        status_enum_test.go
```

`article.go` produced four outputs, one per generator that claimed it,
plus a mock for the interface it references. Each is named
`<source-basename><plugin-suffix>` — which is why they sort next to
the file that caused them.

Open `blog/article_repo.go`:

```go
// Code generated by eidos-reference. DO NOT EDIT.
//
// Source:    blog/article.go
// Plugins:   golang 1.0.0, repogen 1.0.0, …
// Command:   eidos run ./...

package blog
```

The header records what produced it and from what. There is no
timestamp — two runs over unchanged input produce byte-identical
files, which is what makes the next step work.

## 4. Ask why a file landed where it did

```sh
/tmp/eidos explain blog.Article
```

```
Subject:    example.com/demoproject/blog.Article (struct)
Position:   /tmp/tut/blog/article.go:25:6
Directives:
  +gen:repo
  +gen:builder
  +gen:register
Metadata:
  shape.writer.detected = false
Outputs:
  builder:
    blog/article_builder.go        slot:top (builder.type)
  mockgen:
    blog/article_mock_test.go      ArticleRepositoryMock (struct)
  registry-gen:
    blog/article_registry.go       slot:init (registrygen.registration)
  repogen: (2 contributions)
    blog/article_repo.go           ArticleRepo (struct)
    blog/article_repo.go           ArticleRepository (interface)
```

Three things worth noticing.

**The selector is `blog.Article`, not a path.** `explain` takes a
qualified declaration name. Handing it `./...` reports *resolves to no
source or emit entity*, which reads like an empty project and is
really a usage error.

**`Metadata` is not yours.** `shape.writer.detected` was stamped by an
annotator that inspected the type. Generators read those stamps to
decide what applies — that is how plugins cooperate without calling
each other.

**One file, two contributions.** `repogen` put both a struct and an
interface into `article_repo.go`. Several plugins can also write into
one file; `explain` is how you find out which did.

## 5. Watch the drift gate work

`check` runs the pipeline into memory and compares against disk,
writing nothing. It is what you put in CI.

```sh
/tmp/eidos check ./...
```

```
check: no drift detected across 13 output(s)
```

Now edit a generated file the way a hurried colleague would:

```sh
printf '\n// hand edit\n' >> blog/article_repo.go
/tmp/eidos check ./... ; echo "exit=$?"
```

```
drift: /tmp/tut/blog/article_repo.go (content differs)
check: 1 drifting file(s)
exit=5
```

Exit `5` is the drift signal specifically — distinct from `1` (your
invocation was wrong) and `2` (your sources were). CI can tell the
three apart.

Regenerate to fix it:

```sh
/tmp/eidos run ./...
/tmp/eidos check ./... ; echo "exit=$?"    # exit=0
```

## 6. Remove an output

Deleting the directive is how you stop generating something. Open
`blog/comment.go` and delete its `// +gen:builder` line, then:

```sh
/tmp/eidos run ./...
ls blog/comment_builder.go     # still there
```

`run` **never deletes**. It cannot distinguish "no longer generated"
from "not generated by *this* invocation" — you might have run against
one package. Removal is a separate, deliberate command:

```sh
/tmp/eidos prune -dry-run ./...
```

```
would delete: /tmp/tut/blog/comment_builder.go
prune dry-run: 1 would-delete, 0 skipped
```

```sh
/tmp/eidos prune ./...
```

```
deleted: /tmp/tut/blog/comment_builder.go
prune: 1 deleted, 0 skipped
```

`prune` checks each file's generated marker before removing it. A file
the manifest claims but which no longer carries that marker — because
you edited it — is **skipped and reported**, never deleted. That is
the `0 skipped` in the output above.

## What you now know

- Directives are comments; annotated source still compiles standalone.
- `run` adds and updates, `prune` removes, `check` compares and exits
  `5` on drift.
- Output is named from the source basename and lands beside it by
  default.
- `explain <selector>` answers why a file exists and what put it there.
- Generated files carry no timestamp, so unchanged input means
  byte-identical output.
